sections.heading: What are Segment Trees and Fenwick Trees?
sections.content: Both structures answer range queries (such as the sum or minimum of a[l..r]) while still allowing the array to change. A plain prefix sum array answers a range query in O(1) but needs O(n) to rebuild after a single update. Scanning the range each time needs O(n) per query. Segment trees and Fenwick trees (also called Binary Indexed Trees, or BIT) balance the two: both queries and point updates cost O(log n). A Fenwick tree is shorter and faster to write but supports fewer operations. A segment tree is more flexible and handles minimum, maximum, GCD, custom merges and range updates with lazy propagation.

sections.heading: When to Use It
items: Many range queries mixed with updates to individual elements (mutable range sum)
Range minimum, maximum or GCD queries with updates
Range updates (add a value to every element in a range) followed by range queries
Counting how many earlier or later elements are smaller (inversions, count of smaller numbers after self)
Order statistics on a dynamic set (kth smallest)
Prefix sums that change over time
DP optimization where each state needs the best value over a changing range (LIS with values as indexes)
Keywords: range sum query mutable, update and query, count smaller after self, inversions, range minimum, lazy propagation

sections.heading: The Intuition
sections.content: Instead of storing every element or every prefix, store partial answers for blocks whose sizes are powers of two. Any range can be assembled from about log n such blocks, and changing one element only affects about log n blocks that contain it. A segment tree makes the blocks explicit: each node covers a segment and stores its answer, and the children cover the two halves. A Fenwick tree packs the same idea into one array, using the lowest set bit of an index to decide how many elements each cell is responsible for.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
items: Using index 0 in a Fenwick tree: it must be 1-indexed, since i and -i is 0 for i = 0 and the loops never move
Allocating too little memory for a recursive segment tree (use 4 * n)
Using the wrong identity element: 0 for sum, Int.MAX_VALUE for min, Int.MIN_VALUE for max, 0 for gcd
Off-by-one with inclusive versus half-open ranges in queries
Forgetting to push lazy tags before descending, or forgetting to recompute the parent after the recursive calls
Updating with the new value instead of the difference in a Fenwick tree
Forgetting coordinate compression when values are large or negative
Overflowing Int when summing many values (use LongArray)
Querying a Fenwick tree for min or max after values can decrease or increase, which it cannot undo
Calling build on an empty array without a guard

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Segment trees and Fenwick trees give O(log n) range queries and point updates on a changing array
A Fenwick tree is short and fast, best for sums, counts and prefix queries, and it must be 1-indexed
A segment tree handles min, max, GCD and custom merges by storing an answer per segment
Lazy propagation allows range updates: push pending tags down before descending, and rebuild the parent afterward
Counting problems (smaller after self, inversions) use a Fenwick tree over compressed ranks
Choose the identity element carefully (0, infinity or negative infinity) for empty or non-overlapping segments
